question: Implement a tool-dispatch loop: given a fake model that returns either a tool call or a final answer, run the agent loop, executing tools and feeding results back, with a step limit.
thoughtProcess: This is the heart of an agent. I need a loop that repeatedly asks the model for the next step, and if it is a tool call, dispatches to the registered function, appends the result as an observation, and continues; if it is a final answer, returns it. I enforce a max-step limit so the loop always terminates, and I handle unknown tools and execution errors by feeding an error observation back rather than crashing. The model here is an injected callable so the loop is testable without a real LLM.
lineByLine: The context starts with the goal as a user message. The loop runs at most max_steps times, guaranteeing termination. Each iteration asks the model for the next step. If the step is a final answer, it returns immediately. If it is a tool call, it checks the tool exists, returning an unknown-tool error observation if not, otherwise executing the function inside a try/except so a runtime error becomes a caught error observation rather than a crash. Either way the observation is appended as a tool-role message so the model sees it next turn, and the loop continues. If the model never finishes within the budget, the loop returns a clear step-limit error.
timeComplexity: O(steps) model calls, each doing constant dispatch work plus the tool's own cost.
spaceComplexity: O(steps) for the growing context of observations.

alternativeApproaches.title: Add cost and time budgets
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Beyond a step count, track accumulated cost and elapsed time and break when either exceeds a budget, since a step limit alone does not bound expensive or slow loops.
alternativeApproaches.code:
import time
start = time.monotonic()
if time.monotonic() - start > time_limit:
    return "error: time limit exceeded"

alternativeApproaches.title: Support parallel tool calls
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Let the model return a list of independent tool calls and execute them concurrently with asyncio.gather, appending all observations together, to cut latency when the calls do not depend on each other.

followUps.question: Why append the observation as a message instead of just passing the result to the next model call?
followUps.answer: Because the model is stateless and reasons only over the context it receives, so the observation must become part of that context for the model to see it on the next turn. Appending it as a tool-role message both delivers the result to the model and preserves the full history of what happened, the goal, each tool call, and each result, so the model has the complete record to reason over as the loop progresses. This is exactly how the loop closes: an action produces a result, the result enters the context as an observation, and the model's next decision is conditioned on it, enabling multi-step, adaptive behavior. If you passed only the latest result without appending to the context, the model would lose the accumulated history and could not build on prior steps. Structuring observations as messages with a tool role also keeps the conversation well-formed for the model, distinguishing tool outputs from user input and the model's own reasoning.

followUps.question: Why catch exceptions and turn them into observations rather than letting them propagate?
followUps.answer: Because tools call real, unreliable operations that can raise exceptions, and an uncaught exception would propagate up and crash the entire agent loop, ending the task abruptly and discarding all progress. Since failures are routine rather than rare, an agent that crashes on the first tool error would be far too fragile for production. Catching the exception and returning it as a clear error observation keeps the loop alive and, crucially, gives the model a chance to recover: it can correct a bad argument on the next turn, choose a different tool, or report the problem gracefully. This turns failures into recoverable steps within the loop instead of fatal crashes. It also provides a natural place to log the error for monitoring. The one caveat is that you still bound retries and steps so the model cannot loop forever on an unrecoverable error, but for the common case of transient or correctable failures, feeding the error back as an observation is what makes the agent robust rather than brittle.

question: Implement a retry decorator with exponential backoff for flaky tool calls, retrying only on specified transient exceptions.
thoughtProcess: Tools call unreliable services, so I need a reusable retry mechanism. I write a decorator that wraps a function, retries it up to a max number of attempts, and sleeps with exponentially increasing backoff between attempts. I only retry on a configurable set of transient exception types, since permanent errors should fail fast. I add optional jitter to avoid synchronized retries (thundering herd), and I re-raise the last exception if all attempts fail so the caller sees the failure.
lineByLine: retry is a decorator factory taking the max attempts, the base delay, the growth factor, whether to add jitter, and the tuple of exception types worth retrying. The inner wrapper loops, calling the wrapped function and returning its result on success. If it raises one of the retry_on exceptions, it increments the attempt count and re-raises once the max is reached, so failures ultimately surface. Otherwise it computes an exponentially growing delay, base_delay times factor to the attempt power, optionally adds random jitter to desynchronize retries, sleeps, and loops to try again. Exceptions not in retry_on propagate immediately, so permanent errors fail fast.
timeComplexity: O(max_attempts) calls in the worst case, plus the cumulative backoff sleep time.
spaceComplexity: O(1) — only counters and the delay value.

alternativeApproaches.title: Cap the maximum delay
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add a max_delay ceiling so exponential growth does not produce excessively long waits on later attempts, which matters when max_attempts is large.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use a battle-tested library
alternativeApproaches.explanation: In production, prefer a maintained retry library like tenacity, which handles backoff, jitter, retry conditions, logging, and async out of the box, rather than hand-rolling all the edge cases.

followUps.question: Why use exponential backoff and jitter instead of retrying immediately or at a fixed interval?
followUps.answer: Retrying immediately or at a short fixed interval can make things worse when a service is under stress, because a burst of rapid retries piles more load onto an already struggling dependency, potentially prolonging or worsening the outage. Exponential backoff spaces retries out with increasing delays, so the first retry is quick, catching brief blips, while later retries wait longer, giving a genuinely overloaded or recovering service time to stabilize before you hit it again. Jitter adds randomness to the delays so that many clients retrying at once do not all fire simultaneously, which is the thundering-herd problem: without jitter, synchronized retries create repeated coordinated spikes of load that can keep knocking the service over. Adding random variation staggers the retries across clients, smoothing the load. Together, exponential backoff manages the timing per client to be gentle on a recovering service, and jitter decorrelates retries across many clients, which is the standard, well-proven pattern for retrying against shared remote dependencies gracefully.

followUps.question: Why only retry on specific exception types rather than all exceptions?
followUps.answer: Because only transient errors benefit from retrying, while retrying permanent errors wastes time and resources and can mask real problems. Transient exceptions like timeouts, connection errors, and temporary service unavailability are caused by momentary conditions that often clear up, so a retry has a real chance of succeeding. Permanent errors, such as invalid arguments, a resource that does not exist, or an authentication failure, will produce the identical failure on every attempt, so retrying just delays the inevitable while consuming attempts and backoff time, and in an agent it delays feeding the error back to the model that could correct the underlying issue. Retrying all exceptions could also retry genuine bugs, like a programming error in the tool, which should surface immediately rather than being repeated. By restricting retries to a specific set of transient exception types, the decorator retries where it helps and fails fast where it does not, which is both more efficient and clearer, letting non-retryable errors propagate promptly so the caller or the agent loop can handle them appropriately rather than after several pointless attempts.

question: Write a parser that extracts the Thought, Action, and Action Input from a ReAct-style model output.
thoughtProcess: ReAct agents produce a structured trace like 'Thought: ...', 'Action: tool_name', 'Action Input: {json}'. I need to parse these fields out of the raw text so the loop can dispatch the action. I use regular expressions to capture each labeled section, handle the case where the model produced a final answer instead of an action, and parse the action input as JSON when possible, falling back to the raw string. I return a structured dict the loop can act on, and signal clearly when the output is a final answer.
lineByLine: The parser first checks for a Final Answer, which ends the loop, returning a final step if found. Otherwise it extracts the Thought text up to the next Action or Final Answer label, the Action (the tool name) up to the Action Input label, and the Action Input as the remaining text. If no Action is present and it was not a final answer, it raises, since the output is unparseable. The action input is parsed as JSON when it is valid, giving structured arguments, and falls back to the raw string otherwise. The function returns a structured tool_call dict with the thought, action, and parsed input for the agent loop to dispatch.
timeComplexity: O(n) in the length of the text for the regex scans.

alternativeApproaches.title: Prefer native structured tool calls
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Modern models emit tool calls as structured JSON via the API's function-calling feature, so you get parsed name and arguments directly and avoid fragile text parsing. Use ReAct text parsing only when a model or setup does not support native tool calls.

alternativeApproaches.title: Feed parse errors back to the model
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Instead of only raising, return the parse error to the model so it can reformat its output, enabling a bounded self-correction loop when the trace is malformed.
alternativeApproaches.code: return {"type": "error", "message": "could not parse Action; use the Thought/Action/Action Input format"}

followUps.question: Why is parsing ReAct text output more fragile than using native structured tool calls?
followUps.answer: Because text parsing depends on the model producing output in exactly the expected textual format, and models are probabilistic, so they can deviate: mislabeling a field, adding extra prose, omitting the Action Input, wrapping JSON in code fences, or formatting the trace slightly differently, any of which can break brittle regexes. You end up writing and maintaining fragile patterns and fallback handling to cope with all the ways the text can vary, and parse failures still happen. Native structured tool calls, by contrast, use the API's function-calling mechanism where the model emits the call as structured data, often constrained by the schema, so you receive a parsed tool name and validated arguments directly without any text parsing. This eliminates the whole class of formatting-related failures and gives you type-checked arguments. Because of this, native structured tool calls are the preferred approach when available, and ReAct text parsing is mainly a fallback for models or setups that do not support native tool calling. The parser is useful to understand and to have as a compatibility layer, but it inherits the reliability problems of parsing free-form generated text, which structured output was specifically designed to avoid.

followUps.question: Why check for a Final Answer before trying to parse an Action?
followUps.answer: Because a Final Answer signals that the agent is done and the loop should terminate, so it must take precedence over action parsing to avoid misinterpreting a completed response as another tool call. In the ReAct format, the model alternates Thought/Action/Observation steps until it produces a Final Answer instead of an Action, which is the normal termination condition. If the parser tried to extract an Action first, it might either fail because there is no Action, or worse, mis-parse part of the final answer text as an action, causing the loop to dispatch a spurious tool call rather than returning the answer. Checking for Final Answer first cleanly detects the terminal case and returns a final-type result the loop knows to return, ending cleanly. Only when there is no Final Answer does it make sense to parse the Thought, Action, and Action Input for the next tool call. This ordering reflects the control flow of the agent loop: recognizing completion is the priority, and action dispatch is what happens in the non-terminal case, so the parser mirrors that by resolving the final-answer branch before the tool-call branch.

question: Implement a loop-detection guard that stops an agent if it repeats the same tool call too many times in a row.
thoughtProcess: Agents can get stuck repeating the same action without progress, so I want a guard that detects consecutive identical tool calls and signals the loop to stop. I track the last call (name plus arguments) and a running count of consecutive repeats. When a new call matches the previous one, I increment; when it differs, I reset. If the count reaches a threshold, I report that a loop was detected so the agent can break. I normalize the arguments so ordering does not cause false negatives.
lineByLine: The detector stores the repeat threshold, the last call's key, and a consecutive-repeat count. _key builds a stable identity for a call by combining the tool name with its arguments serialized with sorted keys, so two calls with the same arguments in different key order still compare equal. check computes the current call's key; if it matches the previous one it increments the count, otherwise it resets the tracking to the new call with a count of one. It returns True when the count reaches the threshold, signaling the agent loop that the same call has repeated too many times and it should break out.
timeComplexity: O(k) per check where k is the size of the arguments being serialized.
spaceComplexity: O(1) — only the last key and a counter are retained.

alternativeApproaches.title: Detect cycles, not just consecutive repeats
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Track a window of recent call keys to catch alternating loops (A, B, A, B) that consecutive-repeat detection misses, flagging when a short pattern recurs.
alternativeApproaches.code:
from collections import deque
self.history = deque(maxlen=6)
# detect if a subsequence repeats within the window

alternativeApproaches.title: No-progress detection on observations
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Beyond identical calls, detect when repeated calls keep returning the same unhelpful observation, which signals lack of progress even if arguments vary slightly, and break on that instead.

followUps.question: Why serialize arguments with sorted keys when building the call key?
followUps.answer: Because the same logical tool call can be represented by dictionaries whose keys are in different orders, and without normalization those would produce different serialized strings and thus different keys, causing the detector to miss that they are actually the same call. For example {"a": 1, "b": 2} and {"b": 2, "a": 1} are semantically identical arguments, but a naive json.dumps could serialize them differently depending on insertion order, so a repeated call might not be recognized as a repeat. Using sort_keys=True forces a canonical ordering so that any arguments with the same contents serialize to the same string regardless of order, giving a stable, order-independent identity for the call. This ensures the loop detector correctly counts genuine repeats rather than being fooled by cosmetic differences in key ordering. It is a small normalization step, but it matters for correctness of the comparison, since the whole point of the detector is to recognize when the agent is making the same call over and over, and that recognition must be robust to representation differences that do not change the call's meaning.

followUps.question: What kinds of loops does consecutive-repeat detection miss, and how would you catch them?
followUps.answer: Consecutive-repeat detection only catches the case where the exact same call is made several times in a direct row, so it misses more subtle non-progress patterns. The classic one it misses is an alternating cycle, where the agent bounces between two or more calls, like A, B, A, B, A, B, never repeating the same call consecutively but clearly stuck in a loop. It also misses loops where the arguments vary slightly each time but the agent makes no real progress, and cases where different calls keep yielding the same unhelpful observation. To catch these, you track a window of recent call keys rather than just the last one, and detect when a short subsequence or set of calls recurs, flagging a cycle even when repeats are not adjacent. A complementary technique is no-progress detection based on observations: if repeated steps keep returning the same or equivalent results without advancing toward the goal, you break regardless of whether the calls are identical. In practice you combine several signals, consecutive repeats, cyclic patterns over a window, and lack of progress in observations, along with the hard step and cost budgets as backstops, so the agent is protected against the range of ways a loop can manifest rather than only the simplest one.

question: Build a tool registry that lets you register functions with their schemas and dispatch a call by name with validated arguments.
thoughtProcess: Agents need a central place to register tools and look them up when the model calls one. I build a registry with a decorator to register a function along with its schema, a method to list the schemas for sending to the model, and a dispatch method that finds the function by name, checks required arguments, and calls it. Missing tools and missing required arguments are returned as clear errors rather than exceptions so the agent loop can handle them. This is the plumbing that connects model tool calls to real functions.
lineByLine: The registry holds a dict mapping tool names to their function, description, and required-argument list. register is a decorator that records a function under a name with its schema info, returning the function unchanged so it can still be called normally. schemas produces the list of tool descriptions to send to the model so it knows what is available. dispatch looks up the tool by name, returning a clear error if it is unknown, then checks that all required arguments are present, returning a descriptive error listing any missing ones. If validation passes it calls the function with the arguments inside a try/except and returns a structured result, converting any runtime exception into an error rather than crashing.
timeComplexity: O(1) average for lookup, plus O(r) to check r required arguments.

alternativeApproaches.title: Validate full parameter types, not just presence
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Store a richer parameter schema and validate types and constraints (with a library like pydantic or jsonschema) rather than only checking required-field presence, catching wrong-typed arguments before execution.
alternativeApproaches.code:
from jsonschema import validate
validate(instance=args, schema=tool["parameters"])

alternativeApproaches.title: Auto-generate schemas from signatures
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use function introspection and type hints to derive the parameter schema automatically, reducing the risk of the schema drifting out of sync with the actual function signature.

followUps.question: Why have dispatch return structured error results instead of raising exceptions?
followUps.answer: Because in an agent, dispatch failures like an unknown tool or missing arguments are expected, recoverable events that the loop should handle by feeding feedback to the model, not fatal errors that should crash the run. Returning a structured result with an ok flag and an error message lets the caller, the agent loop, uniformly handle both success and failure: on failure it can append the error as an observation so the model can correct its call on the next turn, and on success it uses the result. If dispatch instead raised, the loop would need try/except around every dispatch call, and an unhandled exception could terminate the agent on what is really a routine, correctable mistake. Structured returns also make the outcomes explicit and easy to branch on, and they keep the boundary between untrusted model-generated calls and your code clean, since every failure mode, unknown tool, missing args, runtime exception, is normalized into the same result shape. This design treats tool dispatch as a place where errors are data to be handled rather than exceptions to propagate, which is what makes the agent robust and the control flow simple.

followUps.question: Why does the registry expose a schemas method separate from dispatch?
followUps.answer: Because the two serve different sides of the tool-use cycle and have different consumers. The schemas method produces the tool descriptions that are sent to the model so it knows which tools exist and how to call them; this is the information the model reasons over to decide and construct a tool call. The dispatch method is used after the model has emitted a call, to actually look up and execute the corresponding function with validated arguments. Separating them cleanly divides the concern of advertising capabilities to the model from the concern of executing a chosen call in your code. It also lets you control exactly what is exposed to the model, for example presenting only a relevant subset of schemas for a given request while the full registry remains available for dispatch, which supports dynamic tool selection. And it keeps the registry a single source of truth: the same registration provides both the schema the model sees and the function the code runs, reducing the risk of the description and implementation drifting apart. So the split mirrors the natural flow, schemas out to the model, calls back in for dispatch, and keeps each responsibility focused and independently usable.

question: Implement a function that executes multiple independent tool calls concurrently and returns their results, handling per-call failures without aborting the others.
thoughtProcess: When a model emits several independent tool calls, running them concurrently cuts latency. I use asyncio to run all calls at once and gather their results, but I must ensure one failing call does not cancel the others, so I catch exceptions per call and record them as errors rather than letting gather propagate. I return a list aligned with the input calls, each entry marked as a success with a result or a failure with an error, so the agent can feed all observations back, including partial failures.
lineByLine: run_one handles a single call: it looks up the async tool function by name, returning an unknown-tool error result if absent, otherwise awaiting the function with the given arguments. It wraps execution in a try/except so any failure becomes a structured error result rather than a raised exception, which is key to isolation. run_parallel creates a task for each call and awaits them all with asyncio.gather, so they execute concurrently. Because run_one never raises, one call's failure cannot cancel the others, and gather returns a list of per-call results, each marked ok with a result or not ok with an error, aligned to the input order for the agent to consume.
timeComplexity: O(1) scheduling overhead per call; wall-clock time is roughly the slowest single call rather than the sum.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the n tasks and their results.

alternativeApproaches.title: Add per-call timeouts
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Wrap each call in asyncio.wait_for so a single slow tool cannot delay the whole batch, converting a hang into a timeout error result while the others complete.

alternativeApproaches.title: Thread pool for blocking (sync) tools
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If tools are synchronous and blocking, run them concurrently with a ThreadPoolExecutor via asyncio.to_thread or concurrent.futures, since plain asyncio only overlaps awaitable I/O, not blocking calls.

followUps.question: Why isolate failures per call instead of letting asyncio.gather propagate the first exception?
followUps.answer: Because by default asyncio.gather propagates the first exception and, in doing so, you lose the results of the other calls that may have succeeded, and pending tasks are effectively abandoned, which is the opposite of what a robust parallel dispatch wants. When a model issues several independent tool calls, a failure in one, say a timeout on a single lookup, should not throw away the successful results of the others, since the agent can often proceed with partial results or retry only the failed call. By catching exceptions inside run_one and returning them as structured error results, each call is isolated: one failure becomes a recorded error in that call's result rather than an exception that tears down the whole batch. gather then always returns a complete list of per-call outcomes, successes and failures alike, aligned to the input. This lets the agent feed all observations back to the model, which can then reason about the partial success, ignore or retry the failure, and continue. It mirrors how sequential dispatch turns errors into observations rather than crashes, applied to the concurrent case, and it is what makes parallel tool execution resilient to the reality that some independent calls will fail while others succeed.

followUps.question: When is running tool calls in parallel not appropriate?
followUps.answer: Parallel execution is only appropriate for calls that are truly independent, so it is not appropriate when calls have data dependencies, where one call's arguments come from another's result, since the dependent call cannot start until the first finishes, forcing sequential execution. It is also risky for side-effecting actions that could conflict or must happen in a specific order, for example two writes to the same resource, where running them concurrently could cause race conditions or leave inconsistent state, so those should be serialized or coordinated. You also avoid unbounded parallelism when it would overwhelm a downstream service or exceed rate limits, in which case you cap concurrency rather than firing everything at once. And for blocking synchronous tools, naive asyncio does not actually run them in parallel, so you need a thread or process pool, or the concurrency is illusory. In short, parallelize independent, ideally read-only or non-conflicting calls to gain latency, and fall back to sequential execution whenever there is a dependency, an ordering or consistency requirement, a resource-contention concern, or a rate limit. The determination of independence and safety is exactly what the agent or its runtime must make before choosing to parallelize, since incorrectly parallelizing dependent or conflicting calls trades a latency gain for correctness bugs, which is never a good trade.
